name: Fang (Esaɲan)
autonymMeaning: “those of Ɲan”, the children of Ɲan
overview: The Esaɲan of Minko'o, a Fang majority in their area, live alongside the Bulu, the Zaman and the Baka. Their language extends from Océan and Vallée-du-Ntem to northern Gabon and Congo. Cocoa, livestock, hunting and bushmeat with plantain make up their daily life; every 1 January, the visit to the graves brings the whole village together.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group that overlaps with the Bulu, Zaman and Baka and also speaks their languages.
Fang is spoken in the Océan, the Vallée-du-Ntem, northern Congo, northern Gabon and in Libreville.
Mixed group; both sexes marry outside the group.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land, with no religious significance.
The group came from Akɔfəm and keeps ties with other Fang (Yəmboŋ).

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Cantons and 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-degree chiefdoms; each village, a 3rd-degree chiefdom, brings together families that are all related.
The chief decides after consulting the notables, sometimes by vote, more often by consensus.
Exchanges take place with respect for seniority; the man, as head of the family, guides his wife and children.
Permanent family societies: the Esaɲan dancers lead the eko after burials; the esa minkale, traditional healers, watch over health.
Internal alliances and divisions often follow political movements.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband.
No age for becoming a man: he needs his hut, enough to eat, a plantation and a wife; the young girl becomes a woman through marriage. The wife must simply be younger than her husband.
Steps: presentation (əzu bug mvug), request for the list, bride price, accompanying.
Drink and food mark the village's acceptance of the marriage; the bride price in money is compensation, a form of goodbye.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cult of the dead every 1 January: the “visit to the graves” brings together all the villagers.
Places: the village (ŋiam), ancestral land; the tombs (sɔŋ), resting place of the ancestors; the river (osuaŋ), place of purification.
Birth prolongs life; death takes one back to the ancestors. In case of serious illness, they are consulted through the eboka, a spiritual journey, to find the remedy.
Taboos: striking a parent, lodging a complaint against him, incest. Men do not touch their father's wives; certain meats are forbidden to women, viper to children.
Insulting one's parents brings a curse; striking them means isolation.
One becomes a diviner when a deceased person initiates you in a dream.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Cocoa, livestock rearing, hunting, farming.
The land belongs to the men, who inherit it from their parents or buy it.
Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Wrapper and shirt; obom and panther skin; kaba for women.
Flourishing traditional medicine, in great demand.
Beauty: the strong, tall, robust man; the woman with beautiful hair and beautiful calves.
Courtship: the man offers presents; it is not customary for the woman to make the first move.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: The eko, with tam-tam, drum, obaka (miŋkəŋhə pot lid) and məŋas, accompanies funerals as well as weddings.
Festival: New Year, with visits to the graves, every 1 January.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Visiting graves and the eboka distinguish the Esaɲan, who are otherwise close to the Bulu.

sections.title: The names
items: The father consults his family: the name of a deceased person or of a loved one is often given; the name does not change.
Everyone is called by their name, with the appellative ǎ-: ǎ-Məŋgata for Mengata.
The founding ancestor is called Esa Mba.

lessons.title: Who are the Fang (Esaɲan)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Fang (Esaɲan) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Fang (Esaɲan) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Fang (Esaɲan) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Fang (Esaɲan) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Fang (Esaɲan) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Fang (Esaɲan) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group that overlaps with the Bulu, Zaman and Baka and also speaks their languages. • Fang is spoken in the Océan, the Vallée-du-Ntem, northern Congo, northern Gabon and at Libreville. • Mixed group; both sexes marry outside the group. • Ancestral land, with no religious significance. • The group came from Akɔfəm and keeps ties with other Fang (Yəmboŋ).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Esaɲan of Minko'o, a Fang majority in their area, live alongside the Bulu, the Zaman and the Baka. Their language extends from Océan and Vallée-du-Ntem to northern Gabon and Congo. Cocoa, livestock, hunting and bushmeat with plantain make up their daily life; every 1 January, the visit to the graves brings the whole village together.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Fang (Esaɲan) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Fang (Esaɲan)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Fang (Esaɲan) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Fang (Esaɲan) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Fang (Esaɲan) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Fang (Esaɲan) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Cantons and chiefdoms of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd degree; each village, a 3rd-degree chiefdom, brings together families that are all related. • The chief decides after consulting the notables, sometimes by vote, more often by consensus. • Dealings follow respect for seniority; the man, as head of the family, guides his wife and children. • Permanent family societies: the Esaɲan dancers lead the eko after burials; the esa minkale, traditional healers, look after health. • Alliances and internal divisions often follow political movements.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cantons and 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-degree chiefdoms; each village, a 3rd-degree chiefdom, brings together families that are all related. The chief decides after consulting the notables, sometimes by vote, more often by consensus. Exchanges take place with respect for seniority; the man, as head of the family, supervises wife and children.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Fang (Esaɲan), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Fang (Esaɲan)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Fang (Esaɲan), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Fang (Esaɲan).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Fang (Esaɲan), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Fang (Esaɲan).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: bushmeat and plantain, greens (fɔlɔn, zom, kpem), pistachio dish (nnam ŋgɔn). • Drinks: arki (spirits). • Cocoa, livestock rearing, hunting, farming. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Fang (Esaɲan) mainly eat bushmeat and plantain, fɔlɔn, zom, kpem, nnam ŋgɔn. Traditional drinks: arki. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Fang (Esaɲan): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Fang (Esaɲan)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Fang (Esaɲan) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Fang (Esaɲan) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Fang (Esaɲan) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Fang (Esaɲan) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The father consults his family: the name of a deceased or dear person is often given; the name does not change. • Everyone is called by name, with the appellative ǎ-: ǎ-Məŋgata for Mengata. • The founding ancestor is called Esa Mba. • Birth prolongs life; death brings one back to the ancestors. In case of serious illness, they are consulted through the eboka, a spiritual journey, to find the remedy. • There is no set age for becoming a man: he needs his hut, enough to eat, a plantation and a wife; a girl becomes a woman through marriage. The wife must simply be younger than her husband.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Fang (Esaɲan), traditional dances (funerals, weddings) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum, obaka. Festival(s): New Year and visiting the graves.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Fang (Esaɲan)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Fang (Esaɲan), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Fang (Esaɲan). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Fang (Esaɲan), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Fang (Esaɲan). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Cocoa, livestock rearing, hunting, farming. • Land belongs to men, who inherit it from their parents or buy it. • Ancestral crafts: baskets for carrying harvests.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cocoa, livestock rearing, hunting, farming. Land belongs to men, who inherit it from their parents or buy it.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Fang (Esaɲan)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Fang (Esaɲan)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Fang (Esaɲan), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Fang (Esaɲan). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Fang (Esaɲan), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Fang (Esaɲan). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of the dead every 1 January: the “visit to the graves” brings all the villagers together. • Places: the village (ŋiam), ancestral land; the graves (sɔŋ), resting place of the ancestors; the river (osuaŋ), place of purification. • Birth prolongs life; death leads back to the ancestors. In case of serious illness, they are consulted through the eboka, a spiritual journey, to find the remedy. • Taboos: striking a parent, taking legal action against them, incest. Men do not touch their father's wives; certain meats are forbidden to women, viper to children. • Insulting one's parents brings a curse; striking them brings isolation.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cult of the dead every 1 January: the “visit to the graves” brings together all the villagers. Places: the village (ŋiam), ancestral land; the graves (sɔŋ), resting place of the ancestors; the river (osuaŋ), place of purification.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Fang (Esaɲan) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Fang
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Fang (Esaɲan) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Fang (Esaɲan) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Fang (Esaɲan) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Fang (Esaɲan) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Fang. • Greeting formulae: Mbolo = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mbolo = morning greeting (one person); Mboloane = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: dza, Bibae, Bila, Binin, Bitan. • The founding ancestor is called Esa Mba. • The visit to the graves and the eboka set the Esaɲan apart, who are otherwise close to the Bulu.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Fang are the first steps towards communicating with the Fang (Esaɲan). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Fang.

activities.title: I greet

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Fang are the first steps towards communicating with the Fang (Esaɲan). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
